storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA are fundamentally different in subject matter.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is choosing between B.Com and BBA based on degree titles.

candidates.title: The Title Trap
candidates.audienceGap: Believing degree names define a unique, non-overlapping subject set.
candidates.viewerChange: Moves from title-based guessing to source-based investigation.
candidates.concept: Comparing Semester I course lists from official documents.
candidates.payoff: Student saves time by verifying specific course overlaps.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management appears in both B.Com and BBA Sem I (JOY University 2025-26).

storySpine.startingBelief: Choosing a degree is a test of my academic identity.
storySpine.studentSituation: A student feels pressured to choose a degree that fits their friend's path.
storySpine.observation: Friend's tasks and my preferred tasks are not comparable without testing them.
storySpine.focus: Using tasks to identify personal interest rather than degree fit.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Only by trying a task can you see which specific skill you enjoy.
storySpine.changedAction: Student records a specific task sticking point to ask a mentor.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student feels relieved from the pressure to 'know' and begins a small, practical exploration.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees a supportive, low-pressure approach to academic discovery.

candidates.title: The Sticking Point
candidates.audienceGap: Believing a single task defines academic aptitude or degree choice.
candidates.viewerChange: Shifts from anxiety about 'fit' to curiosity about 'interest'.
candidates.device: A friendly, informal conversation between two peers.
candidates.payoff: Student stops worrying about the degree name and starts looking at the actual work.
candidates.hlni: A short illustrative activity reveals interest, but does not determine degree success.
methodSteps: Perform a short, illustrative course task.
Note exactly where you need help.
Formulate a question about that specific step.
candidates.interpretationRule: The goal is to find what you want to learn next, not to judge the degree.
candidates.visibleProof: A small notebook showing one 'Stuck' point and one 'Question' for the professor.
candidates.limitations: Does not measure aptitude or predict long-term success.

demonstration.input: Attempting to create a small personal budget.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Create a personal monthly budget
demonstration.observation: Student is stuck on how to categorize irregular income.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How do you handle irregular cash flow in these accounting modules?

storySpine.startingBelief: If I pick the wrong degree, I lose my future.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is paralyzed by the fear of making the wrong choice.
storySpine.observation: Preferences are just hypotheses until checked against actual course requirements.
storySpine.focus: Distinguishing between a preference and a verified requirement.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Assumptions create paralysis; verifying requirements creates a path forward.
storySpine.changedAction: Student creates a 'Checklist of Unknowns' instead of a 'List of Preferences'.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student moves from panic to a structured list of verification steps.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees a compassionate, practical way to handle high-stakes academic stress.

candidates.title: The Reality Check
candidates.audienceGap: Treating personal preferences as if they were verified course requirements.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to separate what they want from what they need to verify.
candidates.device: A sticky-note activity on a bedroom wall.
candidates.payoff: Student feels empowered by having a clear list of things to verify.
candidates.hlni: Preference is not confirmation; unknown requirements must be verified as a next step.
candidates.support: Logical distinction between desire and verification.
methodSteps: List your top degree preference.
List the requirements you hope it satisfies.
Mark unknowns as 'To Verify' tasks.
candidates.interpretationRule: Do not treat an option as available until the unknown requirement is confirmed.
candidates.visibleProof: A wall filled with sticky notes, some moved from 'Preference' to 'To Verify'.
candidates.limitations: Never assume eligibility or institutional availability.

demonstration.input: Student writes 'I want to study Finance'.
demonstration.observation: Student realizes they haven't verified if the course covers specific financial modeling.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Does the course offer advanced modeling in the first year?

storySpine.startingBelief: A high-level task description is enough to know what the degree is about.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student sees a 'Business Simulation' task and assumes it belongs to BBA.
storySpine.observation: The same simulation task appears in both B.Com and BBA descriptions.
storySpine.focus: Demonstrating why a single task cannot prove a degree-specific identity.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: General task names don't account for the underlying institutional versioning.
storySpine.changedAction: Student stops labeling the task and searches for the course-specific syllabus source.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student demonstrates that the label 'Business Simulation' is insufficient to differentiate the two degrees.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer is presented with a visual puzzle that challenges their categorisation instincts.

candidates.title: The Unlabeled Task
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming a single task belongs exclusively to one degree.
candidates.viewerChange: Understands that task titles are not unique degree indicators.
candidates.device: A guessing game where the answer is 'not enough information'.
candidates.payoff: Viewer learns to look for the source before making an exclusive claim.
candidates.hlni: One unlabeled example cannot prove degree ownership; it lacks the necessary institutional link.
candidates.support: Logical reasoning: absence of evidence is not evidence of exclusivity.
methodSteps: Show an example task without a source.
List the degrees it could potentially belong to.
Identify the missing source needed to link it.
candidates.interpretationRule: When the link is missing, label it 'Not Enough Information'.
candidates.visibleProof: A card game where the 'Guess' is crossed out and replaced with 'Need Source'.
candidates.limitations: Cannot prove the task exists in either degree without official documentation.

demonstration.observation: There is no source document provided to link this to a specific programme.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the official course document for this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: Two degrees with the same total credits are identical.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student assumes B.Com and BBA are the same because they both have 120 credits.
storySpine.observation: The credit totals are identical, but the breakdown of subjects is different.
storySpine.focus: The hidden difference between aggregate totals and component parts.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Totals hide the underlying mix; comparing components reveals the actual difference.
storySpine.changedAction: Student breaks down the credit structure instead of comparing just the total.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Student discovers the subject mix is what matters, not the credit count.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer experiences a 'aha' moment as numbers are broken down.

candidates.title: The Hidden Breakdown
candidates.audienceGap: Using aggregate numbers to judge degree similarity.
candidates.viewerChange: Shifts from comparing totals to comparing component breakdowns.
candidates.device: Arithmetic manipulation on a digital screen.
candidates.payoff: Viewer avoids the trap of using misleading total metrics.
candidates.hlni: An aggregate total hides the underlying component mix; always request a breakdown.
candidates.support: Mathematical logic of aggregate vs. components.
methodSteps: Display the total credit count for two programmes.
Break down the subject categories within that total.
Compare the specific category mix.
candidates.interpretationRule: Do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
candidates.visibleProof: A bar chart where the same total height is composed of different colored segments.
candidates.limitations: Figures are illustrative and do not represent a specific real-world curriculum.

demonstration.observation: The credit categories (core vs. elective) differ significantly between the two programmes.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the specific breakdown of these 120 credits?

plan.contrast: The selected candidates differ by mechanism: Trust uses documented evidence of shared modules to correct assumptions; Connection uses a reflective journal method to manage personal anxiety; Discovery uses a logical challenge to prove why aggregate labels are misleading. Each addresses a different cognitive gap: curriculum knowledge, emotional management, and logical categorization.

issues: fidelity: The provided evidence (ju-bcom-af-2025-sem1 and ju-bba-em-2025-sem1) only confirms 'Business Organization & Management' as a shared module; it does not contain or support the claim that a 'Business Simulation' task appears in both, creating a factual inaccuracy. Correction: Replace the claim about 'Business Simulation' with the verified fact that 'Business Organization & Management' appears in both programme documents.
